lead: A transmission line carries a forward wave. When the load impedance is not equal to the line's characteristic impedance, part of the wave reflects back. The forward and reflected waves add to make a standing wave. The reflection coefficient measures the reflected wave, and VSWR measures how strong the standing wave is. These numbers tell you how much power reaches the load and how badly a link or antenna is matched.
prereq: You need: characteristic impedance Z0 and propagation constant β from Chapter 1.1.

blocks.text: A load ends a line of characteristic impedance Z0. If ZL = Z0, all incident power is absorbed and no wave returns. If ZL differs, the boundary cannot support the same voltage-to-current ratio as the line, so a reflected wave must exist. The reflection coefficient ΓL is the complex ratio of reflected voltage wave to incident voltage wave at the load.

blocks.where: ZL is load impedance in Ω; Z0 is line characteristic impedance in Ω; ΓL is dimensionless and complex.

blocks.text: For a passive load, |ΓL| lies between 0 and 1. |ΓL| = 0 means a matched load. |ΓL| = 1 means total reflection, as with an open or short circuit. Some books call |Γ| the reflection factor. The phase of ΓL records whether the reflected voltage is in phase or out of phase with the incident voltage.

Move a distance d from the load toward the generator. On a lossless line the magnitude does not change, but the phase rotates. The factor 2 appears because the wave travels d forward and d back, a round trip of 2d.

blocks.where: Γ(d) is reflection coefficient at distance d from the load; ΓL is its value at the load; β is phase constant in rad/m; d is distance toward the generator in m.

blocks.text: The total voltage is the sum of forward and reflected waves. On a lossless line with real Z0, V(d) = V+ e<sup>−jβd</sup>[1 + Γ(d)]. The current is I(d) = (V+/Z0)e<sup>−jβd</sup>[1 − Γ(d)]. V+ is forward voltage amplitude in V. The bracketed terms add or cancel as the phase of Γ(d) changes, so |V| rises and falls along the line.

blocks.where: |V(d)| is voltage magnitude at distance d in V; |V+| is forward voltage amplitude in V; |Γ| is magnitude of load reflection coefficient; θ is phase angle of ΓL in rad; β is phase constant in rad/m; d is distance from load in m.

blocks.text: The largest voltage is Vmax = |V+|(1 + |Γ|). The smallest is Vmin = |V+|(1 − |Γ|). The voltage standing wave ratio is VSWR = Vmax/Vmin = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|). VSWR is real and at least 1. A matched line has VSWR = 1. A short or open line has VSWR = ∞. Invert the formula when you know VSWR: |Γ| = (VSWR − 1)/(VSWR + 1).

Voltage maxima and current minima occur together. Voltage minima and current maxima occur together. Adjacent maximum and minimum are λ/4 apart; the pattern repeats every λ/2. On a lossless line VSWR does not change with d. The figure uses |Γ| = 0.5, so Vmax/Vmin = 1.5/0.5 = 3 and VSWR = 3.

For a real Z0, incident power is P+ = |V+|²/(2Z0). Reflected power is P− = |Γ|² P+. Power delivered to the load is PL = P+ − P− = P+(1 − |Γ|²). The fraction |Γ|² is reflected; 1 − |Γ|² reaches the load. A load with |Γ| = 0.447 reflects 0.20 of the power and delivers 0.80.

blocks.where: RL is return loss in dB; |Γ| is magnitude of reflection coefficient at the reference plane. It is positive for |Γ| < 1. Reflection loss is the same decibel measure in many texts; |Γ| itself is the reflection factor.

blocks.text: Mismatch loss is different: ML = −10 log10(1 − |Γ|²) dB. It is the extra loss caused by mismatch when the source is matched. Line efficiency for the mismatch alone is η = PL/P+ = 1 − |Γ|². This is not the same as conductor and dielectric efficiency. If |Γ| = 0, return loss is infinite dB and all power is delivered. If |Γ| = 1, return loss is 0 dB and no net power reaches the load.

figure.caption: Voltage magnitude on a lossless line with a real load reflection coefficient of 0.5. The maximum is 1.5, the minimum is 0.5, and adjacent maximum and minimum are a quarter wavelength apart.

spec.title: Standing wave on a mismatched line
spec.aria: Voltage magnitude along a line with a real reflection coefficient of 0.5 rises to 1.5 and falls to 0.5 every quarter wavelength.

examples.question: A 50 Ω lossless line is terminated by ZL = 100 + j50 Ω. Find the load reflection coefficient ΓL, its magnitude |Γ|, the VSWR, the return loss in dB, and the fraction of incident power reflected. State the fraction delivered to the load.
steps: Z0 = 50 Ω and ZL = 100 + j50 Ω. Use ΓL = (ZL − Z0)/(ZL + Z0).
Multiply numerator and denominator by 150 − j50 Ω. Numerator = (50 + j50)(150 − j50) = 10000 + j5000 Ω². Denominator = 150² + 50² = 25000 Ω². ΓL = 0.4 + j0.2.
examples.answer: ΓL = 0.4 + j0.2, |Γ| = 0.447, VSWR = 2.62, return loss = 6.99 dB, reflected power fraction = 0.20, and delivered power fraction = 0.80.
examples.check:
from math import log10
ZL = complex(100, 50)
Z0 = 50
G = (ZL - Z0) / (ZL + Z0)
m = abs(G)
vswr = (1 + m) / (1 - m)
rl = -20 * log10(m)
pr = m * m
pt = 1 - pr
print(round(G.real, 3))
print(round(G.imag, 3))
print(round(m, 3))
print(round(vswr, 2))
print(round(rl, 2))
print(round(pr, 3))
print(round(pt, 3))

traps: Treating Γ as a real number: Γ is complex. Its magnitude sets VSWR and reflected power, but its phase sets where the voltage maxima and minima sit.
Writing VSWR = (1 − |Γ|)/(1 + |Γ|): the correct form is VSWR = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|), so VSWR is at least 1 and becomes infinite at total reflection.
Calling return loss negative: return loss = −20 log10|Γ| dB is already positive for a passive load; 6.99 dB is correct, −6.99 dB is not.
Confusing return loss with mismatch loss: return loss uses |Γ| and 20 log, while mismatch loss uses 1 − |Γ|² and 10 log.
Thinking VSWR changes along a lossless line: only the phase of Γ rotates; |Γ| and VSWR stay the same.

quiz.q: Define the load reflection coefficient ΓL and state its formula.
quiz.a: ΓL = (ZL − Z0)/(ZL + Z0), the complex ratio of reflected to incident voltage wave at the load; ZL is load impedance and Z0 is line impedance, both in Ω.

quiz.q: Why does |Γ| stay constant on a lossless line while Γ changes with distance?
quiz.a: The line has no loss, so the reflected wave keeps its amplitude. Travel changes only phase: Γ(d) = ΓL e^(−j2βd), so the magnitude remains |ΓL|.

quiz.q: A 50 Ω line ends in 75 Ω. Find ΓL, VSWR and return loss.
A load gives |Γ| = 0.5. Find VSWR, reflected power fraction and delivered fraction.
A line has VSWR = 2.0. Find |Γ| and return loss. Does a change to VSWR = 1.5 improve matching?
quiz.a: |Γ| = (2 − 1)/(2 + 1) = 0.333. RL = 9.54 dB. At VSWR = 1.5, |Γ| = 0.2 and RL = 13.98 dB; higher return loss means better match, so yes.

quiz.q: For a real positive ΓL, where on the line are voltage maximum and minimum? How far apart?
quiz.a: Voltage maximum at the load, d = 0. Minimum at d = λ/4. Adjacent maximum and minimum are λ/4 apart; the pattern repeats every λ/2.

quiz.q: State the difference between return loss and mismatch loss.
quiz.a: Return loss RL = −20 log10|Γ| dB compares reflected power with incident power. Mismatch loss ML = −10 log10(1 − |Γ|²) dB is the extra loss due to mismatch.

beyond: Not for the exam. In a lab, a vector network analyzer measures S11, which is Γ at the test port; the same numbers become a return-loss trace and a Smith chart plot. Antenna and RF board designers use VSWR and return-loss limits for cellular, Wi-Fi and radar hardware. Search terms: return loss vs VSWR, S11, mismatch loss, voltage standing wave ratio, reflection coefficient phase.
